intro: Linear for computer systems analysts on Mac is mostly about turning stakeholder requests into tracked issues that engineers can act on. Use Linear's templates, intake forms and Mac shortcuts to do that without retyping the same questions. Lazur sits on top of the work. It points at controls, explains them out loud and drafts text while you keep going.
tldr: Use Standard templates for your own team and Form templates for requesters outside it.
Workspace templates cannot preset team labels or statuses, so build a template for each team.
Press C to start an issue, ⌥C to start one from a template and ⌘K to search actions by name.
The Free plan allows 250 issues. Linear's pricing page does not say what happens at that cap.
Lazur points at controls and explains them out loud. It does not click for you.

blocks.text: What a systems analyst does in Linear on Mac

Computer systems analysts sit between the people who need a system and the people who build or run it. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics lists duties such as meeting managers to decide how IT systems can serve the organization. Others include weighing the costs and benefits of upgrades, testing systems, and writing manuals for end users. Each duty becomes work you track in Linear. A request becomes an issue. A test plan becomes sub-issues. A user guide becomes a linked document.

For most analysts, the work is sorting and writing more than coding. That is why your Linear setup matters as much as your technical skill. Asana says 60% of a person's time at work goes to 'work about work' rather than skilled work. Its Anatomy of Work Index surveyed over 10,000 knowledge workers. The page does not say which year the survey covers, so treat the figure as a rough signal, not a benchmark.
Set up intake templates so requests arrive complete

Linear has three issue template types: Standard, Form and Default. A Form template collects structured input when someone creates the issue. You can require any field. That makes Form templates the right tool for requests from people outside your team, such as finance or operations.

Read the docs for its exact behavior before you rely on it.
blocks.caption: Linear's three issue template types and how to use them

blocks.text: Linear's docs also say Form templates work as default templates only for non-team members. Plan your intake around that rule. Keep Standard templates for your team and send outside requesters to the form. The split keeps internal issues quick and outside requests complete.

A form that asks for the business reason, the deadline and the owner is less likely to need follow-up questions. Ask for one thing per field. Long free-text boxes produce vague requests. Short fields with clear labels produce usable issues on the first pass.
Team templates and workspace templates

Workspace templates cannot preset team-specific properties. Team labels and issue statuses are the common examples. Team templates appear only when you create an issue in that team. Build one team template for each team that files this work. A single workspace template cannot cover all of them.

Two more rules matter. A sub-issue can use only templates that do not contain sub-issues. If you used Asks-field templates before, Linear migrated them to form templates. Linear offers a best-effort conversion back to standard templates.

blocks.title: Check the template scope
blocks.text: Before you edit a template, check whether it is a workspace or a team template. Team templates show up only inside their team, so a missing one is often in the wrong team.
Keyboard shortcuts for creating and finding issues on Mac

Press C to open the issue creation modal. Press ⌥C to create an issue from a template. Linear's docs say linear.new redirects to the creation page, so you can bookmark it as a fast start. Those three entry points cover most intake days.

blocks.text: The ⌘N behavior changed on September 3, 2026. Cmd or Ctrl plus N now lets you choose what to create from the current view. If you learned ⌘N as 'new issue,' test it once. You may get a menu instead. Keep C or ⌥C for the direct route.

Use ⌘K when you forget a shortcut. The command menu searches actions by name. Linear upgraded its fuzzy search on September 3, 2026. On October 22, 2026, Create new loop joined the menu. Type a few letters of the action name and let the menu find it.

Numbered shortcuts also changed. Since the March 12, 2026 UI refresh, Cmd or Ctrl plus number works on non-US keyboard layouts. If you type on a French or German layout, test the numbers once so you know they fire.
Safari Tab focus and lost drafts in Linear

If you create issues in Safari, Tab can jump focus unexpectedly. Linear's docs point to a Safari setting as the fix. Open Safari > Settings > Advanced. Turn on 'Press Tab to highlight each item on a webpage.' Then test Tab in the issue form before you rely on it.
Unsaved drafts are stored locally on your Mac. Logging out, restarting or resetting Linear clears them. Save long text in a note before you restart. Restarting is the easiest trigger to forget.

blocks.title: Drafts do not survive a restart
blocks.text: Logging out, restarting or resetting Linear clears unsaved issue drafts. Copy long descriptions somewhere safe before you restart or sign out.
Hand an issue to an AI coding tool on Mac

If your engineers use an AI coding tool, open an issue and press ⌘⌥. (Command, Option and the period key). Linear opens the tool with a prompt already filled in. The prompt includes the issue ID, the description, the comments and linked references. Press W, then O, to choose from the tools your workspace has enabled.

Check the prompt before you send it. Comments often hold side debates, customer names or pricing notes. The shortcut fills the prompt. It does not check what is in it. Read the comments the way you would before sharing a spec outside the team.

Screenshots often explain a bug faster than a long description. Linear's changelog says the macOS desktop slash menu gained an Insert screenshot option on September 24, 2026. Type / in the description, pick Insert screenshot, and attach the screen where the report broke.
Inbox and priority settings when everyone pings you

Priority inbox, dated September 3, 2026, adds a Priority tab. It separates notifications that need attention from those that can wait. Linear chooses the defaults. You can pick which notification sources feed the tab, or create a filter for the people who escalate most.

A practical routine: open the Priority tab first thing, then work through the rest of the Inbox after your first meeting. Mute the sources that send noise. Keep one filter for stakeholders whose messages always need a reply. Review that list once a month.

Comments need care too. Since March 12, 2026, you can send comments with Enter or with ⌘Enter, depending on your preference. Choose the setting that matches how you write. If Enter sends, a stray keypress can post a half-finished reply.
Views, reviewer complaints and what to plan around

Read the complaints before you commit a team to Linear. A Product Hunt roundup of Linear reviews counted the most-cited cons. Confusing structure came up 10 times. The missing kanban board came up 8 times. Single task assignment came up 6 times, and limited customization came up 5 times.
Those counts are small and self-selected. Treat them as warning signs, not verdicts. The same roundup listed performance as a pro, not a complaint. Your own test matters more than the average review.

One reviewer says Linear defaults to the 'active' view. Someone who does not notice may think they see the full sprint. Check the view name in the header before you report status. A wrong view means a wrong number in a stakeholder update.

blocks.title: Board view claim
blocks.text: The roundup says Linear has no kanban board. This page did not open Linear's board documentation, so check the layout options in your own workspace before you promise one.

Plan for the structure complaint directly. Name each view after the question it answers, such as 'Intake this week.' Write down which filter is the team's working list. Share that list in one place so people stop building their own.
Plan limits and which Linear plan a small analyst team needs

Linear's Free plan lists $0 with 2 teams, 250 issues and 10MB file uploads. Paid plans are per user. Basic is $10 per user per month, and Business is $16 per user per month, both billed yearly. Enterprise is custom and billed annually. Count the people who create and edit issues before you pick a tier.

blocks.text: The Free plan has one gap. The pricing page does not say what happens when you reach 250 issues. Some third-party blogs claim creation gets blocked after a downgrade. This page did not verify that. Ask Linear before a team builds a real project on the Free plan.

blocks.title: Compare the yearly cost
blocks.text: Multiply the per-seat price by the number of people who edit issues, then compare that yearly total with your budget. Linear's pricing page lists Basic and Business as billed yearly, so check their pricing page for any other billing option.
How Lazur helps while you work in Linear

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. Hold ⌥ ⌘, which is Option and Command together, and ask about anything on screen. Lazur answers out loud. Ask where a control is and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do something and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click.

Lazur does not click for you. It does not edit files or operate other apps. It is not a plugin or add-in for Linear, and it has no partnership with Linear. You keep the mouse and the keyboard. Lazur explains what is on screen and types text where you ask it to.

Dictation works separately. Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app, including Linear's issue description. Snippets, a personal dictionary and clipboard slots handle repeat text, such as a standard acceptance criteria block. Dictation is unlimited on both paid plans. See [Lazur plans](/pricing).

Research is the other background job. Lazur runs research in its own Chrome tabs, through the Lazur for Chrome extension. It returns a summary and a report. Use it when a question sends you through several vendor pages, such as comparing plan limits. Lazur keeps a memory of what you asked and did, stored on your Mac.

Privacy is simple to state. Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers so Lazur can answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available.
A worked example: from a stakeholder email to a tracked issue

Here is one Monday. An operations lead emails that the weekly order export is missing a column. The lead works outside your team, so you send a form link instead of starting a thread. This is a worked example, not a measured result. It shows where each Linear feature fits.

items: Send the Form template link. Mark the report name, the missing column and the deadline as required.
Open a team template for exports with ⌥C. Pick the one that sets your team's labels and statuses.
Hold fn and dictate the acceptance criteria into the description. Read it back before you save.
Add sub-issues for the query change and the test. Use a template that has no sub-issues, since sub-issues cannot use templates that contain them.
If an engineer uses an AI coding tool, open the issue and press ⌘⌥. Read the prompt before you send it.
Stuck on a control? Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask Lazur where the label field is. Lazur circles it.

blocks.text: The analyst's own time went to two decisions. Which column does the export need? When is it due? Linear handled the tracking. The templates handled the repeat questions. Your job was the judgment in between.
Mistakes systems analysts make in Linear

items: Building one workspace template for every team, then wondering where the labels went. Team labels need a team template.
Sending outside requesters a Standard template. They skip fields, and you end up chasing them later.
Leaving required fields unmarked. A form with no required fields lets blank requests through.
Restarting Linear with a long draft open. Save the draft first.
Reporting sprint status from the wrong view. Check the view name first.
Sending an AI coding prompt before you read the comments.

faq.question: Does Linear work on a Mac?
faq.answer: Yes. Linear has a desktop app for macOS, and its changelog lists Mac-only changes such as Insert screenshot in the macOS slash menu. Linear also runs in a browser, and its docs cover Safari.

faq.question: What is the difference between a Standard template and a Form template?
faq.answer: Linear's docs list Standard, Form and Default as template types. A Form template collects structured input when someone creates the issue, and you can require any field. Use Form for people outside your team.

faq.question: Can I use Lazur to fill in a Linear issue?
faq.answer: Lazur can dictate text at your cursor with fn and draft text for you to paste. It does not click buttons or operate Linear. You still fill in the fields and save the issue yourself.

faq.question: Does Lazur plug into Linear?
faq.answer: No. Lazur is not a plugin or add-in for Linear, and it has no partnership with Linear. It looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut, and it answers out loud.

faq.question: What happens when a Free plan workspace reaches 250 issues?
faq.answer: Linear's pricing page lists the 250-issue limit but does not say what happens at the cap. Ask Linear before you depend on the Free plan for a live project.

faq.question: Why might my team report different sprint status?
faq.answer: One reviewer says Linear defaults to the active view. Check the view name in the header before you report status, and agree on one view for stakeholder updates.

faq.question: Does Lazur work on Windows for Linear?
faq.answer: Not yet. Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available.
